scenes.title: A day of research
scenes.caption: In 2024, researchers published an average of 9,600 science and engineering papers a day. For someone outside the field, even a single figure can be hard to follow.

scenes.title: Imagine Science
scenes.caption: Imagine Science is an open-source tool that uses AI agents to turn research into animations more people can understand.

scenes.title: From paper to storyline
scenes.caption: It starts with a paper. The agent traces each claim back to its source, then builds a storyline around what the audience needs to see.

scenes.title: Writing the scene
scenes.caption: The agent writes the scene in TypeScript. React describes the parts of the figure. SVG draws the shapes and labels. Remotion controls how they change from one frame to the next.

scenes.title: Matching voice to action
scenes.caption: Next, ElevenLabs generates one continuous voice track. The timing of each phrase tells the agent where to place the captions and when to cue the motion. When the narrator says the particles spread, the cloud opens up on screen.

scenes.title: Rendering the film
scenes.caption: Once the timing is set, Remotion renders the frames in a browser. FFmpeg stitches them together and adds the narration to create the final MP4.

scenes.title: Checking the export
scenes.caption: Then the agent checks the export. It verifies the frame count, dimensions, and audio track, then compares individual frames with the source. Watching the film all the way through reveals things a still frame can miss.

scenes.title: Correcting a cue
scenes.caption: If a label arrives late, or a movement suggests something the paper doesn’t support, the agent changes the scene in code and renders it again.

scenes.title: Explore Imagine Science
scenes.caption: Check out Imagine Science on GitHub!

assets.source: ElevenLabs Bella (hpp4J3VqNfWAUOO0d1Us), eleven_multilingual_v2, English narration with a separately recorded closing sentence. Stability 0.48, similarity 0.78, speed 1. Word cues use provider character timestamps. FFmpeg, SVG, and MP4 use spoken spellings.
